sections.title: Taxonomy and symbiosis
sections.text: Parmelia sulcata Taylor (1836) is a foliose lichen in the family Parmeliaceae, not a crustose lichen. Its thallus is formed by an ascomycete fungus associated with a photobiont, here a chlorococcoid green alga. The lobes usually form a rosette attached to bark or rock.

sections.title: Thallus and upper surface
sections.text: The thallus most often forms a distinct 4–10 cm rosette, sometimes reaching 20 cm. Its grey to whitish-grey, narrow, flattened lobes are about 2–5 mm wide and may overlap. The upper surface bears a raised network of elongated pseudocyphellae that crack or pit the surface. Granular, pale grey, powdery soralia develop in lines along this network and may spread toward the centre of the thallus. Isidia are absent.

sections.title: Lower surface and reproduction
sections.text: The lower surface is black and bears numerous black rhizines that anchor the thallus to its substrate; they range from simple to forked, with some branched into small tufts. Reproduction is mainly vegetative, through soralia that disperse soredia containing both the fungus and its algal partner. Apothecia are rare; when present, they are disc-shaped with a brown disc and a margin often bearing soralia.

sections.title: Habitat and range
sections.text: A common epiphyte on the bark of many trees, it also grows on wood and sometimes rock. It tolerates varied environments and occurs from lowlands to higher elevations depending on region; sources also report acidic or subacid substrates. Its range is very broad, spanning several continents. Among close relatives, Parmelia saxatilis is distinguished in part by isidia rather than the linear soralia of P. sulcata.

traits: Grey to whitish-grey foliose lichen, usually in a 4–10 cm rosette, sometimes up to 20 cm; flattened lobes 2–5 mm wide.
Raised network of elongated pseudocyphellae on the upper surface; powdery soralia line the ridges and can spread across the centre.
Black lower surface with numerous black rhizines, simple, forked or sometimes in small tufts.
Reproduces mainly by soredia in the soralia; rare brown apothecia often have a sorediate margin.
Common epiphyte on tree bark, also found on wood and sometimes rock; very wide distribution.
